\section[\hi{कृपया}]{\hi{कृपया} (kṛpayā) — please (kindly)}

\label{lesson:HI-C08-kripaya}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Hindi's dictionary word for "please" is really the word \textbf{compassion} in disguise — and it's more formal than you might expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} = \textbf{please}, literally "\textbf{kindly / graciously}." It's built on the Sanskrit noun \textbf{\hi{कृपा}} (\emph{kṛpā}), "\textbf{grace, compassion, mercy}" — so asking with \emph{kṛpayā} means, at heart, "of your compassion."

That places Hindi in good company: \textbf{Arabic} asks \emph{min faḍlik} ("from your \textbf{grace}"), and the Dravidian languages ask with \emph{daya} ("\textbf{compassion}"). A whole swathe of Asia says \emph{please} by naming the kindness it hopes for — a different instinct from French's "if it \textbf{pleases} you."

The first letter hides a sound you met in the syllabary track: \textbf{\hi{कृ}} is \emph{ka} carrying the \textbf{vocalic r} (the \emph{\hi{ृ}} mark) — \emph{kṛ}, the same \emph{ṛ} vowel Sanskrit and the Dravidian scripts share.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about how it's used}
Here's the catch a textbook often hides: \textbf{\hi{कृपया} is formal and bookish.} You'll see it on signs and hear it in announcements ("\emph{kṛpayā} mind the gap"), but in everyday speech Hindi speakers rarely say it. Real politeness usually rides on \textbf{the verb} instead — the respectful request ending \textbf{‑\hi{इए} / ‑\hi{इएगा}} (\emph{-iye / -iyegā}): \emph{baiṭh\textbf{iye}} "please sit," \emph{sun\textbf{iye}} "please listen." And very often, people simply say the English word \textbf{"please."}

So learn \emph{kṛpayā} to \textbf{read} it and to be formally polite — but know that the living "please" of Hindi is baked into the verb.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "kṛpayā" — kṛ with the vocalic r, then -payā{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the root — "kṛpā = compassion" $\to$ "of your compassion"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the everyday way — the verb ending: "baiṭhiye" = "please sit"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What is the formal Hindi word for please? (\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} \emph{kṛpayā}.) What does its root \emph{kṛpā} mean, and which other languages ask the same way? (\textbf{"Grace / compassion"} — like Arabic \emph{min faḍlik} and Dravidian \emph{daya}.) Is \emph{kṛpayā} what people usually say out loud? (\textbf{No} — it's formal; everyday politeness rides on the verb ending \emph{-iye/-iyegā}, or people say English "please.")
\end{tcolorbox}
